mainTopic: When an admission of debt is binding, and when it may be written into a document
overview: This amud is about when an admission of a debt really counts. It starts with a man who admitted a debt casually and later said 'it never happened.' One view calls him a כפרן, but רבא's version says people simply forget casual remarks. Next come stories of lenders who hid witnesses to catch an admission. From them we learn that an admission counts unless the borrower openly says 'no' to being witnessed. Then come cases about people who talk about debts so they won't look rich, including a deathbed admission on which רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי and רבי חייא ruled differently. The גמרא then asks when witnesses may write an admission into a document: with a קנין, before three people acting as a בית דין, and for land as opposed to movables. It ends with the wording of admission documents. The amud closes as a new case about a document called 'a record of the proceedings' begins; that case continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Denying that the admission ever happened makes him a liar
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of a ruling: if the defendant says 'these things never happened,' he is established as a כפרן.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says 'these things never happened,' he is established as a denier (a liar about his debts).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ruling about someone who admitted a debt casually and then went to court. If in court he says the admission never happened at all, he is treated as a liar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses heard him admit, so when he says 'it never happened,' he is contradicting what they heard. This marks him as a כפרן. A person with that status is not trusted to take a שבועה to free himself from payment.

keyTerms.meaning: He is established as / gets the status of
A denier: someone who falsely denies what he owes
'These things never happened': a full denial

steps.confusionAlert: Saying 'it never happened' is different from saying 'I was only joking.' Here the problem is that he denies the admission completely, even though witnesses heard it.

phrases.english: 'These things never happened' —
phrases.notes: He means: 'I never admitted any such thing.'

phrases.english: he is established as a denier.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא הָיוּ דְבָרִים מֵעוֹלָם הוּחְזַק כַּפְרָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ruling that began before this section of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who fully denies an admission that witnesses heard is treated as a כפרן.

steps.title: Another version: people forget casual remarks
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא son of רב אחא בר אדא reports in the name of רבא that the denier is not a liar, because people do not remember casual things.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא, son of רב אחא בר אדא, said: This is how we say it in the name of רבא: people do not remember all casual matters.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא brings a different tradition from רבא that disagrees with the ruling in step 1.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The admission was said casually, not seriously. So when the man later says 'it never happened,' he may simply have forgotten it. In that case he is not lying, and he does not become a כפרן.

keyTerms.meaning: This is how we say it in his name: a different version of a teaching
Casual matters, things said without serious intent

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא's version, forgetting a casual remark is normal, so a later denial is not proof of lying.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא,
phrases.english: Rav Pappa, son of Rav Aḥa bar Adda, said:
This is what we say in the name of Rava:
all casual matters —
people do not remember.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי אָמְרִינַן מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the ruling of step 1, using a different tradition from רבא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects calling the man a כפרן when he denies a casual admission.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 1 assumes the denial is a lie. In fact he may honestly have forgotten something he said casually.

steps.title: Witnesses hidden in the bed canopy
steps.stepSummary: A lender hid witnesses in his canopy. The borrower admitted the debt but refused to let 'those awake and asleep' be witnesses. רב כהנא rules that his 'no' cancels the admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man hid witnesses in his canopy to hear his friend. He said: 'I have a מנה in your hand.' The friend said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Let those awake and those asleep be witnesses about you.' The friend said: 'No.' רב כהנא said: He told him 'no.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a trap set to catch an admission of debt, and gives רב כהנא's ruling on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower did say 'yes, I owe you.' But when he was asked to let listeners serve as witnesses, he refused. רב כהנא rules that because he said 'no' to having witnesses, his 'yes' does not obligate him to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Canopy or curtain over a bed
A sum of one hundred דינרים

phrases.english: There was a certain man who hid witnesses
for his fellow, in his canopy.
phrases.notes: He hid them in the curtain over his bed so they could secretly hear the conversation.

phrases.english: He said to him: 'I have a maneh in your hand.'
He said to him: 'Yes.'
He said: 'Those awake and those asleep —
let them be witnesses about you.'
He said to him: 'No.'
Rav Kahana said:
But he said to him 'no'!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דְּאַכְמֵין לֵיהּ עֵדִים לְחַבְרֵיהּ בְּכִילְּתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new case about admissions that do not obligate.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An admission is not binding when the speaker explicitly refuses to let listeners be witnesses to it.

steps.title: Witnesses hidden in a grave
steps.stepSummary: A lender hid witnesses in a grave. The borrower admitted the debt but refused to let 'the living and the dead' be witnesses. רבי שמעון בן לקיש rules the same way: his 'no' cancels the admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man hid witnesses in a grave to hear his friend. He said: 'I have a מנה in your hand.' The friend said: 'Yes.' 'Let the living and the dead be witnesses about you.' The friend said: 'No.' רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: He told him 'no.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second, almost identical story, and the ruling is the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The setup is the same as before, only now the witnesses are hidden in a grave. Again the borrower refused to accept witnesses, so his 'yes' does not obligate him. A second אמורא gives the same ruling, which strengthens the rule from step 3.
steps.whatToRemember: In both stories the rule is the same: if he says 'no' to being witnessed, his earlier 'yes' does not obligate him, even though witnesses actually heard it.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who hid witnesses
in a grave, for his fellow.
He said to him: 'I have a maneh in your hand.'
He said to him: 'Yes.'
'The living and the dead —'
let them be witnesses about you.'
He said to him: 'No.'
Rabbi Shimon [ben Lakish] said:
phrases.notes: Some versions just say רבי שמעון; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording, naming ריש לקיש.

phrases.english: But he said to him 'no'!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דְּאַכְמֵין עֵדִים בְּקִיבְרָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story that gives the same ruling as step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Refusing to be witnessed cancels the binding force of an admission, as in the canopy case.

steps.title: Silence would have made the admission count
steps.stepSummary: רבינא (or רב פפא) learns from the hidden-witness cases that the rule of רב יהודה in the name of רב, that one must say "you are my witnesses," is met even if only the lender says it and the borrower stays silent.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא, and some say רב פפא, said: Learn from these cases that the rule of רב יהודה in the name of רב, that someone must say "you are my witnesses," works whether the borrower says it or the lender says it while the borrower stays quiet. The borrower in those cases was free only because he said "no." If he had stayed silent, the admission would count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a practical rule out of the two hidden-witness stories. It asks who has to say "you are my witnesses" for an admission to count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה in the name of רב taught that an admission counts only if someone says "you are my witnesses." From steps 3 and 4 we learn that the lender saying it is enough, as long as the borrower stays silent. The borrower escaped there only because he openly said "no."

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it, a conclusion drawn from earlier cases
"You are my witnesses," the words that make an admission legally binding

steps.whatToRemember: An admission counts if the lender says "you are my witnesses" and the borrower stays silent. Only an open "no" from the borrower cancels it.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the borrower himself must say "you are my witnesses." Staying silent while the lender says it is just as good.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule for when an admission in front of witnesses obligates the borrower.

phrases.english: Ravina said, and some say Rav Pappa said:
Learn from this:
phrases.notes: "This" means the two hidden-witness cases just told, in the canopy and in the grave.

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: That which Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
One must say, "You are my witnesses"
It makes no difference whether the borrower said it

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא שְׁנָא כִּי אָמַר מַלְוֶה וְשָׁתֵיק לֹוֶה.
phrases.english: or whether the lender said it and the borrower stayed silent.
The reason he was free is that the borrower said "no"
but if he had stayed silent, then indeed the admission would count.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ מֵהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rule from the two hidden-witness rulings in steps 3 and 4.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that "you are my witnesses" can be said by the lender while the borrower stays silent
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rulings of רב כהנא and רבי שמעון בן לקיש, where only the borrower's open "no" cancelled his admission

steps.title: The man nicknamed 'a קב of debts'
steps.stepSummary: A man known as a heavy debtor said that only two named people had claims on him. Those people sued him before רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man people called "a קב of debts." He said: Who has claims on me except so-and-so and so-and-so? Those people came and sued him in court before רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about a casual admission of debt. It sets up רב נחמן's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man named people he owed, but he said it casually and not to them as witnesses. The question is whether this offhand remark counts as a real admission.

keyTerms.meaning: "A kav of debts," a nickname for someone known to owe many people
Has a claim of money against me

phrases.english: There was a certain man whom they called "a kav of debts"
phrases.notes: A קב is a measure of volume. The nickname means he was loaded with debts.

phrases.english: He said: Who has a claim of money on me
except so-and-so and so-and-so?
They came and sued him in court
before Rav Nachman.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּהֲוָה קָרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case about an admission that may not have been meant seriously.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case. The ruling comes in the next step.

steps.title: People downplay their wealth
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules the man is not liable, because people tend not to show themselves as wealthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: A person tends not to make himself look rich.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן rules on the "קב of debts" case. The man's remark does not obligate him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People often claim to owe money so others won't think they are wealthy. So a casual statement like this is not a real admission, and he does not have to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: A person tends to (normal human behavior)
To make himself look "full," meaning wealthy

steps.whatToRemember: A casual claim to owe money is not a binding admission, because people like to look less wealthy than they are.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:

phrases.aramaic: אָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: A person tends not to make himself look wealthy.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: אָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for the case told in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A casual admission of debt does not obligate, since people tend to downplay their wealth.

steps.title: The man nicknamed 'a mouse lying on dinars'
steps.stepSummary: A known miser said on his deathbed that two named people had claims of money on him. After he died, they sued his heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man people called "a mouse lying on dinars." When he was dying, he said: So-and-so and so-and-so have claims of money on me. After he died, they came and sued the heirs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about an admission of debt, this time made on a deathbed. This step only sets up the case. The ruling comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This man was a miser who looked poor while sitting on money. He made his admission while dying, and the people he named now claim it from his heirs. The question is whether his words bind them.

keyTerms.meaning: "A mouse lying on dinars," a nickname for a miser who guards money he never uses

phrases.english: There was a certain man whom they called
"a mouse lying on dinars."
When he was dying, he said:
"So-and-so and so-and-so have claims of money on me."
After he died,
they came and sued the heirs.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּהֲווֹ קָרוּ לֵיהּ עַכְבְּרָא דְּשָׁכֵיב אַדִּינָרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case to step 6, but a deathbed admission by a miser instead of a casual remark.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case. The ruling follows in the next part of the sugya.

steps.title: A deathbed admission is believed
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי rules that the idea that people hide their wealth applies only during life, not on the deathbed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They came before רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי. He said to them: When we say 'a person tends not to show himself as wealthy,' that is only during his lifetime. After death, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The heirs of the miser and the two claimants come to court, and רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי rules in favor of the claimants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7, רב נחמן let a living man off because people make up debts to look poor. רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי limits that reasoning to a living person. A man about to die has no reason to look poor, so his words are taken as true.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'to make himself full,' meaning to show himself as wealthy
This applies only to... (a limiting phrase)
After death; here it means a statement made on the deathbed

phrases.aramaic: אֲתוֹ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי.
phrases.english: They came before Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.
He said to them: When we say
'A person tends not to show himself as wealthy,'
phrases.notes: This is the reason רב נחמן gave back in step 7.

phrases.english: that applies during his lifetime,
but after death, no.
phrases.notes: He means words said on the deathbed, which counts as 'after death' here.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אָמְרִינַן אָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ הָנֵי מִילֵּי מֵחַיִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the deathbed case set up in step 8, and limits רב נחמן's reasoning from step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The idea that people hide their wealth does not apply to a deathbed statement, so the admission is binding.

steps.title: A second judge says a father hides his sons' wealth
steps.stepSummary: After the heirs pay half, the claimants sue for the rest, and רבי חייא rules that a man also hides the wealth of his children.
steps.simpleTranslation: They paid half. Then the claimants sued them in court for the other half. They came before רבי חייא. He said to them: Just as a person tends not to show himself as wealthy, so too a person tends not to show his sons as wealthy.
steps.whatsHappening: The story goes on: the heirs paid half, the claimants sued for the second half, and רבי חייא rules against the claimants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא widens the reasoning of step 7. Even a dying man has a reason to make up debts: he does not want his sons to look rich. So for the second half, the deathbed admission does not obligate the heirs.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי חייא does not deny that people hide their own wealth. He adds that people also hide their children's wealth. That is why the deathbed does not change things for him.

phrases.english: They paid half,
they sued them in court for the other half.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתוֹ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא. אֲמַר לְהוּ:
phrases.english: They came before Rabbi Chiya. He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ,
phrases.english: Just as a person tends not to show himself as wealthy,

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת בָּנָיו.
phrases.english: so too a person tends not to show his sons as wealthy.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת עַצְמוֹ כָּךְ אָדָם עָשׂוּי שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ אֶת בָּנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ruling that goes against step 9's limit on the reasoning of step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A deathbed admission may be untrue, because a father wants his sons to look poor, so the heirs are not liable.

steps.title: The heirs ask to undo the first payment
steps.stepSummary: The heirs ask רבי חייא whether they can now reverse the earlier ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Should we go and reverse it?
steps.whatsHappening: The heirs ask a follow-up question that sets up רבי חייא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא's view means the heirs never owed anything. So they ask whether they can get back the half they already paid under the first ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us reverse it or take it back

phrases.english: They said to him: Should we go and reverse it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ נֵיזִיל וְנַיהְדַּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from רבי חייא's ruling in step 10 and asks what it means for the payment made under step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can the first ruling be reversed so the heirs get their money back?

steps.title: An elder already ruled, so the first ruling stands
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא refuses to reverse the earlier ruling because an elder already gave it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: An elder has already ruled.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא answers that he will not overturn what רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי already decided.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though רבי חייא disagrees, the first ruling was given by a respected elder. The first half stays paid, and only the second half follows רבי חייא's view.
steps.whatToRemember: Two judges ruled differently on the same deathbed admission. The heirs paid half under the first ruling and owed nothing more under the second, and the first ruling was not undone because 'an elder already ruled.'

phrases.english: He said to them: An elder has already ruled.
phrases.notes: The 'elder' is רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי, who gave the first ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּבָר הוֹרָה זָקֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the heirs' question from step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. A ruling already given by an elder is not reversed.

steps.title: An admission before two witnesses is written only with a קנין
steps.stepSummary: If someone admits a debt before two witnesses, they may write it into a document only if a קנין was made.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he admitted before two people and they made a קנין with him, they may write it down. If not, they may not write it down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new rule about when witnesses to an admission of debt may write it into a signed document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A written document gives the lender more power than a debt that is only spoken. A קנין shows the borrower agreed to make the admission formal. Without one, the witnesses may not turn his spoken words into a document.

keyTerms.meaning: In front of two people (two witnesses)
They made a קנין with him, a formal act that confirms the matter
They write it down as a document

phrases.english: If he admitted before two,
and they made a קנין with him, they write,
and if not, they do not write.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹדָה בִּפְנֵי שְׁנַיִם וְקָנוּ מִיָּדוֹ כּוֹתְבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new subject that is still about admissions of debt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses may write down an admission they heard only if a קנין was made.

steps.title: Admission before three without a קנין: רב אמי and רב אסי argue
steps.stepSummary: When the admission is made before three people without a קנין, רב אמי says they may write it and רב אסי says they may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he admitted before three people and they did not make a קנין with him: רב אמי says they may write it down, and רב אסי says they may not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a disagreement about an admission made in front of three people when no קנין was done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three people can form a בית דין, and a בית דין may write down what it decides. רב אמי treats the three as a court, so they may write. רב אסי says the borrower may have meant them only as witnesses, so the rule for witnesses in step 13 applies.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who says they write
An אמורא who says they do not write

phrases.english: Before three, and they did not make a קנין with him.
Rav Ami says: they write,
and Rav Asi says: they do not write.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּפְנֵי שְׁלֹשָׁה וְלֹא קָנוּ מִיָּדוֹ רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר כּוֹתְבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the rule of step 13 and asks about a case with three people instead of two.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute: רב אמי says three people may write it down even without a קנין, and רב אסי says they may not.

steps.title: In a real case, רב was concerned for רב אסי's view
steps.stepSummary: In an actual case, רב took רב אסי's view into account and did not let them write the document.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a case, and רב was concerned for this view of רב אסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the dispute with a real case, where רב was careful to follow רב אסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'He was concerned for' means רב did not fully reject רב אסי's view and acted carefully because of it. So in practice, an admission before three people without a קנין was not written down.

keyTerms.meaning: He was concerned for it, he took that view into account

steps.whatToRemember: An admission before two people is written down only if there was a קנין. Before three people without a קנין there is a dispute, and in practice רב was careful to follow רב אסי and not write it.

phrases.english: There was a case,

phrases.aramaic: וְחַשׁ לַהּ רַב לְהָא דְּרַב אַסִּי.
phrases.english: and Rav was concerned for this view of Rav Asi.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲוָה עוֹבָדָא וְחַשׁ לַהּ רַב לְהָא דְּרַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the practical outcome of the dispute in step 14.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In practice, they do not write down an admission made before three people without a קנין, out of concern for רב אסי's view.

steps.title: Who gathered the three people decides whether we write
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה says an admission before three is written only if the debtor himself gathered them, not if they were already sitting together.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: with an admission document, sometimes we write it and sometimes we don't. If the three were already gathered and sitting there, we don't write it. If the debtor gathered them himself, we do write it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה explains when an admission made in front of three people may be written down as a document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three people can count as a בית דין, but only if the debtor meant them to act as one. If he brought them together himself, that shows he wanted a court. If they just happened to be sitting there, maybe he was only talking.

keyTerms.meaning: An admission document: a written record that someone admitted owing money
They were already gathered and sitting

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
This admission document,
phrases.notes: He means the case from before: someone admits a debt in front of three people without a קנין.

phrases.english: sometimes we write it
and sometimes we do not write it.
If they were already gathered and sitting, we do not write it;
if he gathered them himself, we write it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה: הָא אוֹדִיתָא, זִימְנִין כָּתְבִינַן וְזִימְנִין לָא כָּתְבִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the admission-before-three case from the רב אמי and רב אסי dispute by setting a condition for writing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An admission before three may be written only if the debtor himself gathered them.

steps.title: He must say 'be my judges'
steps.stepSummary: רבא says gathering the three is not enough; the debtor must tell them, 'Be judges for me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: even if he gathered them himself, we don't write it unless he tells them, 'Be judges for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא disagrees with רב אדא בר אהבה and asks for more before the document may be written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, gathering people does not prove the debtor wanted a court; maybe he only wanted witnesses. He has to say clearly that they should act as his judges.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Be judges for me': appointing them as a court

phrases.english: Rava said:
Even if he gathered them himself, we do not write it,
unless he says to them: "Be judges for me."

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ כַּנְפִינְהוּ אִיהוּ – לָא כָּתְבִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a stricter requirement than רב אדא בר אהבה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The document may be written only if the debtor explicitly appoints the three as judges.

steps.title: The full court procedure is needed
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי says even 'be my judges' is not enough; the three must act like a real court by setting a place and summoning him.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי said: even if he said 'Be judges for me,' we don't write it unless they set a place, send for him, and summon him to court.
steps.whatsHappening: מר בר רב אשי gives the strictest view: the three must actually run a court procedure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words alone might not be serious. Only when the three set up a place and formally summon the debtor is it clear that his admission was made in a real בית דין, so it can be written.

keyTerms.meaning: They set a place (for the court)

phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi said:
Even if he said: "Be judges for me,"
we do not write it unless they set a place,
and send for him, and summon him to court.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ אָמַר ״הֱווֹ עֲלַי דַּיָּינֵי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes one step stricter than רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a full court procedure (fixed place, sending for him, summons) allows writing the admission.
steps.whatToRemember: Three rising levels: he gathered them (רב אדא בר אהבה), he said 'be my judges' (רבא), or a real summons to court (מר בר רב אשי).
steps.confusionAlert: These three views do not argue about whether a בית דין may write an admission. They argue about what makes the three people count as a בית דין in the first place.

steps.title: Admission about movables needs a קנין
steps.stepSummary: If he admitted a debt of movable items and a קנין was done, it may be written; without a קנין, it may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he admitted owing movable items and they made a קנין with him, they write it. If not, they don't write it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks at the type of property admitted: here, movable items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For movables, a written record needs a קנין, because the קנין makes the admission a firm commitment. Without one, no document is written.

keyTerms.meaning: And they made a קנין (formal act of acquisition) with him

phrases.english: If he admitted regarding movable property,
and they made a formal act of acquisition with him, they write it;
and if not, they do not write it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹדָה בְּמִטַּלְטְלֵי, וְקָנוּ מִיָּדוֹ – כּוֹתְבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from 'who heard the admission' to 'what kind of property was admitted'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An admission about movables may be written only with a קנין.

steps.title: What about land without a קנין?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the law is when he admitted regarding land and no קנין was made.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it was about land and they did not make a קנין with him, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question that sets up the disagreement in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Movables clearly need a קנין. The question is whether land is different, since land is always there to collect from. Maybe that makes the admission firm enough even without a קנין.

phrases.english: Regarding land, and they did not make a formal act of acquisition with him, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The words 'if he admitted' carry over from the line before.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּמְקַרְקְעֵי, וְלֹא קָנוּ מִיָּדוֹ, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the movables rule to a new case, land, and asks whether it still holds.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an admission about land without a קנין may be written.

steps.title: אמימר and מר זוטרא disagree
steps.stepSummary: אמימר says they may not write it; מר זוטרא says they may.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: they do not write it. מר זוטרא said: they do write it.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give opposite answers to the question about land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אמימר treats land like movables, so no קנין means no document. מר זוטרא holds that an admission about land may be written even without a קנין.

phrases.english: Ameimar said: They do not write it.
Mar Zutra said: They write it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר אָמַר: אֵין כּוֹתְבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question with two opposing opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A dispute: אמימר says no writing; מר זוטרא says writing is allowed.

steps.title: The law: we write it
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה follows מר זוטרא: an admission about land may be written even without a קנין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the law is: they write it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the dispute in favor of מר זוטרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So movables need a קנין before the admission is written, but land does not. That is the practical ruling.

phrases.english: And the law is: they write it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא: כּוֹתְבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute from the previous step.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An admission about land may be written into a document even without a קנין, unlike movables.
steps.whatToRemember: Movables: write only with a קנין. Land: write even without a קנין (the הלכה follows מר זוטרא).

steps.title: Are movables that still exist treated like land?
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי בר רב הונא asks רבינא how to treat an admission about movable items that are still physically there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא came to דמהריא. רב דימי בר רב הונא of דמהריא asked him: If someone admits he owes movable items that are still there and intact, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is asked. We already learned that land may be written without a קנין and movables may not, so now someone asks about movables that are still sitting there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land can be written without a קנין because it is always there to collect from. Movables that still exist are also available right now, so maybe they belong with land. The question is which side they fall on.

keyTerms.meaning: Happened to come, arrived at a place
They still exist in their original form

phrases.english: Ravina happened to come to Damharya.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב דִּימִי בַּר רַב הוּנָא
phrases.english: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna said to him
(Rav Dimi of Damharya) to Ravina:
Movable items that are still there and intact, what is the law?
phrases.notes: He means an admission about these items made without a קנין, like the cases right before this.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִטַּלְטְלִי וְאִיתַנְהוּ בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a middle case between movables (step 19) and land (steps 20-22).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an admission about movables that still exist may be written without a קנין, like land.

steps.title: רבינא: they are like land
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that movables still in existence are treated like land.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: They are like land.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the question: movables that still exist are treated like land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the הלכה follows מר זוטרא that an admission about land may be written without a קנין, this answer means these movables may also be written without a קנין.

phrases.english: He said to him: They are like land.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כִּמְקַרְקְעֵי דָּמוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Movables still in existence are treated like land, so the admission may be written.

steps.title: רב אשי: not like land, since they have not been collected
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי disagrees: because the items still need to be collected, they are not like land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי says: Since they still lack collection, no, they may not be written.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives the opposite answer to the same question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי says the items still have not been handed over to the creditor. Until they are collected, they are not as secure as land, so the witnesses may not write the admission without a קנין.

keyTerms.meaning: They are missing, they still lack

phrases.english: Rav Ashi says:
Since they still lack collection, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כֵּיוָן דִּמְחַסְּרִי גּוּבְיָינָא, לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבינא's answer in step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Movables still in existence are not like land, because they have not yet been collected.

steps.title: An admission document missing 'he told us to write'
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא say a document of admission missing the line 'he told us: write, sign, and give it to him' falls under ריש לקיש's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an admission document that did not say 'He told us: write, sign, and give it to him.' אביי and רבא both said: This is the case of ריש לקיש.
steps.whatsHappening: A new case: an admission document is missing the line saying the person asked the witnesses to write it. אביי and רבא say ריש לקיש's rule answers this, and the גמרא will quote that rule next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses may not write an admission unless the person asks them to. Here the document does not say he asked. אביי and רבא connect this to ריש לקיש, which will show that the document is still valid.

keyTerms.meaning: A document recording someone's admission of a debt
Write, sign, and give it to him

phrases.aramaic: הָהִיא אוֹדִיתָא דְּלָא הֲוָה כְּתִב בַּהּ
phrases.english: A certain admission document in which was not written
"He said to us: Write, sign, and give it to him,"
Abaye and Rava both said:
This is the case of Reish Lakish.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא אוֹדִיתָא דְּלָא הֲוָה כְּתִב בַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about the wording of an admission document.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An admission document is not ruined just because it leaves out 'he told us to write'; ריש לקיש's rule applies.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: witnesses only sign when things were done properly
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש's rule: we assume witnesses only sign a document if the deal was done by an adult, even if the document doesn't say so.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: There is a חזקה that witnesses do not sign on a document unless it was done by an adult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes ריש לקיש's rule to explain what אביי and רבא meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses are trusted to sign only when everything was done properly, even if the document doesn't spell it out. In the same way, we assume the witnesses wrote the admission only because the person asked them to, so the missing line doesn't matter.

keyTerms.meaning: A presumption, what we assume happened

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a document is trusted to have been done properly even when not every detail is written in it.

phrases.english: As Reish Lakish said:

phrases.aramaic: חֲזָקָה אֵין הָעֵדִים חוֹתְמִין עַל הַשְּׁטָר,
phrases.english: There is a presumption that witnesses do not sign on a document
unless it was done by an adult.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind אביי and רבא's ruling.
steps.raayaObject: The validity of an admission document missing 'he told us to write'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's חזקה that witnesses only sign when the deal was done properly.

steps.title: רב פפי: would the scribes know what the חכמים don't?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפי (or רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע) challenges: can we assume court scribes know a rule that even the חכמים don't all know?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפי objects, and some say it was רב הונא son of רב יהושע: Is there something that we don't know, and the court scribes do know?
steps.whatsHappening: Someone attacks אביי and רבא's use of ריש לקיש's rule for this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש's rule works for a well-known rule like being an adult. But the rule that an admission needs 'he told us to write' is not known even to all the חכמים. So we can't assume the scribes made sure of it.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (it was someone else)

phrases.english: Rav Pappi objects to this,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua:

phrases.aramaic: מִי אִיכָּא מִידֵּי דַּאֲנַן לָא יָדְעִינַן,
phrases.english: Is there anything that we do not know,
phrases.notes: "We" means the חכמים, who don't all know this rule.

phrases.english: and the scribes of the court do know?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב פַּפֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי and רבא's use of ריש לקיש in steps 26-27.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי and רבא's ruling that ריש לקיש's חזקה covers a missing 'he told us to write'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חזקה only works for rules everyone knows. This rule isn't even known to all the חכמים, so the scribes can't be assumed to follow it.

steps.title: The scribes of אביי and רבא were tested and knew the rule
steps.stepSummary: The scribes of אביי and of רבא were asked about the rule, and both groups knew it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked the scribes of אביי, and they knew. They asked the scribes of רבא, and they knew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from the previous step by reporting a real test: the court scribes were asked, and they knew the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 28 asked how we can assume scribes know a rule that even some חכמים don't know. The answer is that this is a real-life fact, not a guess: the scribes were questioned and they knew. Writing documents is their profession, so they know the laws that apply to it.

keyTerms.meaning: Scribes (here, the court scribes who wrote documents)

steps.whatToRemember: A professional scribe can be assumed to know the laws of his own work, even laws that not every scholar knows. So אביי and רבא's application of רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ's rule stands.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is saying the scribes are greater scholars than the חכמים. It only means they know the specific rules of their own job.

phrases.english: They asked Abaye's scribes, and they knew.
phrases.notes: They knew the rule asked about in step 28: witnesses only write up an admission if he told them to write, sign and give it.

phrases.english: They asked Rava's scribes, and they knew.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁאֵילִינְהוּ לְסָפְרֵי דְאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the קשיא of Step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual answer: the assumption was tested in practice and found true.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Court scribes cannot be expected to know a rule that even some חכמים don't know.
steps.terutzMaskana: The scribes were tested and did know the rule, so we can rely on them to follow it.

steps.title: A new case: a document of admission called 'a record of the proceedings'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a story about a document of admission that was written up as 'a record of the proceedings.'
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain document of admission in which it was written: 'A record of the proceedings,'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new case and is setting up the next move. The sentence continues in the following text, where we will hear what the question about this document was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The document calls itself 'a record of the proceedings,' meaning a write-up of what was said in front of the signers. The sentence breaks off here, and the details of the case and the question about this document continue on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: A document of admission (where someone admits he owes money)
A record of the proceedings (literally, a memory of the words)
That certain one (opens a story about a real case)

phrases.english: A certain document of admission
in which it was written
'A record of the proceedings,'

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא אוֹדִיתָא דַּהֲוָה כְּתִב בַּיהּ דּוּכְרַן פִּיתְגָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After closing the discussion about scribes, the גמרא opens a new real-life case about the wording of a document of admission.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This step only describes the case: a document of admission written as 'a record of the proceedings.'
